title: Best Soft Serve in Sonoma County: 9 Places To Try
summary:
Our dining editor spent the summer tasting Sonoma County’s soft serve, from creamy classics and chocolate-dipped cones to chef-driven desserts and over-the-top toppings. Here are the favorites.

The post Best Soft Serve in Sonoma County: 9 Places To Try appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
You can learn a lot about soft serve by taste-testing nearly every cone in the county. I did exactly that this summer.

First, not all soft serve is created equal. Some is thicker, some airier, some icier; even when two places use the same base, the results can be radically different. Second, Sonoma County’s dairies make some very good soft serve. And finally, I have yet to meet a twist cone I didn’t fall at least a little bit in love with.

Most of Sonoma County’s soft-serve machines use a liquid base from either Straus Family Creamery or Valley Ford Creamery. We’re more than a little spoiled to have either: Both make exceptional dairy.

This list is strictly about dairy soft serve. No yogurt, sorbet, custard or anything else that comes out of a machine and requires its own category. So don’t come at me with your little plastic spoons.

Here are the results of my very unscientific tour of Sonoma County’s soft-serve scene.

Absolute Best Soft Serve: Valley Ford Creamery

The highest praise I can give a dessert is “last-meal good,” and this velvety, butterfat-rich soft serve qualifies. Valley Ford Creamery uses milk from its own Jersey cows to make gelato-smooth vanilla and chocolate soft serve at its cafe and cheese-aging facility. The herd’s high-fat milk gives the frozen dessert a texture that is dense, silky and remarkably easy to keep eating. You may be ruined for lesser soft serve.

14390 Valley Ford Road, Valley Ford, 707-875-7073, valleyfordcheese.com

Most Interesting Toppings: Altamont General Store

Grilled pickled pineapple may be the strangest soft-serve topping on this list, but don’t dismiss it before you try it. Its sweet-tart acidity is excellent with creamy vanilla. Try the Pineapple Express, with organic soft serve, grilled pickled pineapple, passion fruit syrup and sea salt. Other toppings include olive oil, vegan chocolate cookies and gluten-free tahini brownie.

While you’re there, don’t miss the Umami Cloud: miso caramel cold foam dusted with caramel salt over iced chai. Chef’s kiss.

3703 Main St., Occidental, 707-874-6053, altamontgeneralstore.com

Most Committed: Valley Swim Club

Valley Swim Club takes its soft serve seriously. This isn’t a dessert tacked onto the menu; it’s a pillar of the casual, seafood-centric operation. If you’re a cone person, rainbow sprinkles, cookie crumbles, toasted peanuts and white chocolate chips are good choices. Sea salt and olive oil, caramel and chocolate sauce are better contained in a cup. But you do you. The soft serve also makes an excellent shake.

18709 Arnold Drive, Sonoma, 707-243-3032, valleyswim.club

Best Float: River Electric

Of course you’ll want a root beer float while lounging by the pool. Creamy vanilla soft serve and Boylan’s not-too-sweet root beer make an ideal summer combination. Add a shot of bourbon, and you have a relaxation strategy, even with a million kids screaming nearby.

16101 Neeley Road, Guerneville, 707-937-8915, theriverelectric.com

Best for Dip Cones: Foster’s Freeze

Don’t ask what makes that perfect chocolate shell around soft serve so good. You probably don’t want to know. Just order the dip cone and remember childhood: those blistering summer days when Mom and Dad drove to Foster’s Freeze to keep you and your siblings occupied for a while. Oh, the good old days. Even as an adult, accept that some chocolate will probably end up on your shirt. And your shoes. That’s part of the experience.

855 Sebastopol Road, Santa Rosa; 1400 Fourth St., Santa Rosa. fostersfreeze.com

Most Cheffy: Dead Letter

The newish Sonoma restaurant takes soft serve into fine-dining territory, finishing its vanilla swirl with dark-chocolate hard shell and sesame-honeycomb candy. It’s fancy without taking itself too seriously, with plenty of nods to childhood.

101 E. Napa St., Sonoma, 707-933-3665, deadlettersonoma.com

Best Twist: Handline

I have a suspicious number of $7.13 charges from Handline on my credit-card statement this summer. They’re all for the same thing: a large chocolate-and-vanilla twist from the soft-serve window. Those brown-and-white swirls became my post-kayaking reward, hot-day cool-down and “I made it through Monday” consolation. Worth every cent. Usually eaten in my car.

935 Gravenstein Highway S., Sebastopol, 707-827-3744, handline.com

Best Olive Oil: Bravas Bar de Tapas

Delicate tangerine olive oil is a surprising topping to the velvety vanilla soft serve, the savory-sweet combo tastes like the fanciest creamsicle you’ve ever had. If you’re a sweet-on-sweet person, the deep cajeta-style caramel topping takes burnt-sugar sweetness to another level. 420 Center St., Healdsburg, 707-433-7700, barbravas.com

Best Brittle: Grossman’s

Grossman’s serves soft serve with its own collection of toppings, including candied strawberries, white-chocolate crumble, Bubbies brittle and tahini caramel. 308 Wilson St., Santa Rosa, 707-595-7707, grossmanssr.com

Best Affogato: Diavola Pizzeria & Salumeria

A shot of hot espresso poured over cold soft serve is perhaps the best argument for dessert after lunch. The combination of melting soft serve and strong coffee is hard to resist, particularly when you need an afternoon pick-me-up. Eat it with a spoon, then drink whatever’s left.

21021 Geyserville Ave., Geyserville, 707-814-0111, diavolapizzeria.com

How soft-serve machines work

Eating this much soft serve means eventually getting into the mechanics of the machine, because a few settings can mean the difference between an icy mess and a dense, creamy swirl.

Soft serve begins as a liquid mix that is chilled, churned and aerated inside the machine. As the mix freezes, a scraper sweeps it out of the freezing chamber while incorporating air, a process known as “overrun.” That air is a big part of what gives soft serve its characteristic texture.

Most commercial soft-serve machines target an overrun of roughly 30% to 60%. In other words, a gallon of liquid mix can produce about 1.3 to 1.6 gallons of soft serve.

Machines can be calibrated for different temperatures, consistencies and amounts of air. More air produces a lighter, fluffier swirl; less produces something denser and richer.

The mix itself matters, too. Fat and sugar affect how the base freezes and melts, which helps explain why two shops using the same dairy mix can produce noticeably different results. One may hold a tall, firm twist; another may be softer and silkier.

title: New Sonoma County Restaurants To Eat at Right Now
summary:
More than a dozen new restaurants have opened or are on the way in Sonoma County. Here’s where to eat now and what to keep an eye on.

The post New Sonoma County Restaurants To Eat at Right Now appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Keeping up with Sonoma County’s restaurant scene is a full-time job, and this summer I’ve been racing from Healdsburg and Sebastopol to Sonoma and Santa Rosa to try to keep pace. More than a dozen new restaurants have opened in recent weeks, with more on the way. That’s a lot of new menus to work through. Here’s what’s open, what’s coming and where you might want to make your next reservation.

Now open

Dead Letter

The latest restaurant from the team behind the girl & the fig brings a dose of drama to Sonoma’s 19th-century post office, just off the plaza. A Spanish charcoal grill anchors a menu that moves from chicken karaage with hummus to butterflied trout with red curry, with plenty of dishes designed for sharing. The dim, art-filled dining room has a postal-noir sensibility, with surreal digital screens, vintage touches and even a $5 Art-o-mat vending machine. Dinner, apparently, can come with a little diversion. 101 E. Napa St., Sonoma, deadlettersonoma.com

Café Carrusel

Owner Ivy Reyes has turned childhood dreams of an Easy-Bake Oven, clouds of glitter and carousel horses into a Mexi-brunch cafe that makes Barbie’s Dreamhouse look restrained. The six-page menu mixes American and Latin flavors with carnival theatrics: consommé-soaked birria tacos hang from a clothesline; a butterfly-shaped brunch board arrives with pancakes, waffles, French toast and Nutella; and cocktails are topped with fluffy pink cotton candy. This is food designed for fun rather than fine dining, with plenty of glazes, marshmallows and chocolate. Because everyone deserves a little glitter-topped make-believe. 630 Third St., Santa Rosa, 707-655-8365, instagram.com/cafe_carrusel

Capriciano Osteria

Sonoma County has no shortage of Italian restaurants, so a new one needs to give diners a reason to add another to the list. Capriciano Osteria has found one in chef Baki Bekci, whose background includes Four Seasons kitchens and the founding of Mezzaluna. He brings a fine-dining sensibility to Italian-American staples, from warm focaccia and burrata salad to fresh pasta, chicken Parmesan and risotto. Among the standouts are lemon ravioli, grilled octopus and a seafood risotto loaded with shrimp, lobster and clams. 505 Mendocino Ave., Santa Rosa, 707-800-7904, capriciano.com

Dolce Rosa Cafe

I’m not here to defend $20 avocado toast. But if you’re going to spend $20 on it, Santa Rosa’s Dolce Rosa Cafe makes a persuasive case. The all-day cafe gives familiar dishes a fine-dining gloss, from housemade focaccia piled with avocado, burrata, pistachios and hot honey to tiramisu pancakes with espresso mascarpone. A pistachio latte comes rimmed with crushed nuts. Owners Josie Ortega and Martin Chaparro are still tinkering with the menu, which also includes pastas, breakfast burritos and eggs in purgatory. Dinner service may be coming later. 4910 Sonoma Highway, Suite B, Santa Rosa, 707-931-4625, instagram.com/dolcerosacafe

Spur Saloon

Batwing doors, saddle seats, cocktails and 10-gallon-hat fun: Spur Saloon is Windsor’s new country-Western bar. More details are coming next week. 9000 Windsor Road, Windsor, instagram.com/spur.saloon.windsor

Bonnie Bagels & Co.

A small Sebastopol cafe may have finally cracked the code on East Coast bagels in Sonoma County. Bonnie Bagels opened in mid-August with kettle-cooked bagels — boiled and baked, as they should be — that are crisp on the outside, chewy on the inside, and, best of all, available in salt. Owner Michael Sousa and executive chef Greg Kalergis offer the familiar lineup of bagels, schmears, and sandwiches, along with more California-leaning flavors like cheddar-jalapeño and Asiago. The shop occupies the former Hippizzazz pizza space across from HopMonk. 280 S. Main St., Sebastopol, 707-503-6520, bonniebagels.com

The Porch

Chef Lisa Boisset is obsessive about making nearly everything at her tiny Sebastopol bistro from scratch, from stocks and sauces to dressings and focaccia croutons. Even the ketchup gets a multistep treatment: tomatoes are charred, then combined with warm spices, apple cider vinegar and balsamic vinegar. The result makes the Parmesan- and parsley-topped pommes frites particularly difficult to share. Tucked beside Patisserie Angelica and behind the Rialto Cinemas, the modest brasserie serves straightforward, comforting food without much fuss. Its west county porch feels more like a roadhouse than the Parisian Left Bank. 6811 Laguna Park Way, Sebastopol, 707-393-9488, theporchkitchen.com

Wylde Provisions Co.

At this Sebastopol playground cafe, parents can sit in the shade with a proper espresso — or a beer — and a chef-made tofu soba noodle bowl while their children run wild. The menu ranges from yogurt parfaits with blueberry sauce to a giant carnitas sandwich with refried lentils and tomatillo-fish-sauce vinaigrette. But bowls are the specialty, with new combinations appearing weekly. Recent options include the Tamariana Grande, with tamari-glazed turkey sausage over udon with edamame, charred zucchini, pickled ginger and cashew-tamari vinaigrette, and the Chipotle Off the Old Block, with chipotle chicken or tofu, quinoa, black beans, corn and greens in avocado-cilantro dressing. Good food, even if you’re not chasing a toddler. 500 Robinson Road, Sebastopol, instagram.com/wyldeprovisionsco

Hazel

Sometimes when one door closes, another opens — in this case, a 150-year-old yellow clapboard Victorian overlooking downtown Occidental. Less than a year after closing their original location, owners Jim and Michele Wimborough have reopened their decade-old restaurant in the former Barley & Hops space down the street. The airy dining room, with its 19th-century details and tucked-away nooks, already feels like a neighborhood gathering place. The menu remains recognizably Hazel, with wood-fired pizzas, hearty seasonal dishes and the unfussy hospitality that has made the restaurant a west county favorite. 3688 Bohemian Highway, Occidental, 707-874-6003, restauranthazel.com

Also on the radar

Three Cultures Kitchen: Open for nearly a year, this Guerneville restaurant combines Mexican, Salvadoran and American influences with elaborate plating. Crispy pork belly with yucca mash and chicken mole are among the draws. 16218 Main St., Guerneville, 707-604-7031, threecultureskitchen.net

Cloverdale Supper Club: The restaurant at the boutique Cloverdale House Inn aims for a Sinatra-era atmosphere, with steaks, seafood and classic martinis. 240 N. Cloverdale Blvd., Cloverdale, 707-669-5072, instagram.com/supperclubcloverdale

Kyoto Ramen and Hawaiian BBQ: This California-Pacific Rim chain serves 15 types of ramen, along with poke bowls, curry, rice bowls, katsu and kalua pork. 1940 Piner Road, Suite 600, Santa Rosa, 707-888-2906

Jamerikan Jerk: The longtime Jamaican food-truck operator has opened a brick-and-mortar restaurant at 2792 Fourth St. in Santa Rosa. 707-755-1289, jamerikanjerksr.com

Marela: This Italian-inspired restaurant at the rebranded Liora Estate, formerly Hotel Les Mars, replaces Arandas. 27 North St., Healdsburg, 707-473-8030, marelahealdsburg.com

Sonoma Eats: Owners Efrain Balmes and Hayley Cutri have opened a Sonoma location of their Mexican restaurant in the former La Hacienda space. The restaurant is still settling into its new direction, with more of Balmes’ Oaxacan family recipes expected soon. 561 Fifth St. W., Sonoma, 707-996-1783

Just opened

Afghan Kabob Cafe: The second location of the popular Tracy-based halal restaurant serves kabobs, biryani, bolani and more. 2478 W. Third St., Santa Rosa, 707-575-9296, instagram.com/afghankabobcafe

Aladdin Grill: Opening this week, the restaurant will serve traditional wraps, kabobs and Turkish coffee. 2101 W. College Ave., Santa Rosa, 707-500-2024

Coming soon

Olives and Agave: Now slated for mid-September, this restaurant will serve tapas and Mediterranean dishes inspired by Spain and the Middle East in Montgomery Village’s former Cascabel space. 909 Village Court, Santa Rosa, olivesandagave.com

Wild Poppy: The west county cafe known for plant-forward breakfasts and brunch is expanding to a second location at The Barlow, taking over the former Woodfour Brewing space. Plans include a tofu factory in the former brewery room. 6780 Depot St., Suite 160, Sebastopol, thewildpoppycafe.com

Hapa’s on the Mainland: From the Sweet T’s team and pitmaster George Ah Chin, this Hawaiian restaurant is planned for the rebuilt Cricklewood site, with indoor dining and expansive outdoor patios. Expect casual island fare and tiki-style cocktails. Construction is underway. 4618 Old Redwood Highway, Santa Rosa, hapasmainland.com

Mansoor: The former Gravenstein Grill space has changed hands and will become a restaurant focused on live-fire cooking. 8050 Bodega Ave., Sebastopol

title: Lynmar Estate Is a Lush Garden Retreat Minutes From Sebastopol
summary:
The Russian River winery tempts visitors with elegant Pinot Noir and Chardonnay alongside flower-filled gardens.

The post Lynmar Estate Is a Lush Garden Retreat Minutes From Sebastopol appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
There’s no hustle or bustle at Lynmar Estate. Set just a few miles from downtown Sebastopol, the Russian River Valley winery has a knack for whisking visitors away from everyday life with natural beauty and warm hospitality.

The story

San Francisco native Lynn Fritz spent his childhood summers on the Russian River. In 1980, as the founder of a global logistics company, he bought Quail Hill Vineyard near Sebastopol as a family retreat.

The Russian River Valley property came with 30 acres of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay vineyards, which officially made Fritz a grape grower. Winemakers Merry Edwards, then working at Matanzas Creek, and Tony Soter, at Etude, were among his early clients.

Fritz had no intention of starting a winery of his own, but perhaps the story of the estate’s original owner had a subtle influence: Gold Rush prospector Lewis Meyer made the first wine at the site in the 1880s. With the help of winemaker Daniel Moore, Lynmar Estate produced its inaugural vintage in 1994.

Fritz and his wife, Anisya, made Quail Hill Vineyard their permanent home in 2008, and together they now run the day-to-day operations of the winery and tasting room. Over the years, Quail Hill’s Pinot Noir and Chardonnay plantings have expanded to 44 acres, all certified organic. The winery produces about 10,000 cases a year.

Wine isn’t the couple’s only passion. In 2001, after Lynn sold his logistics company to UPS, the couple co-founded the Fritz Institute, a nonprofit logistics organization that helps deliver relief supplies to disaster-stricken communities around the world.

The vibe

Higher-end wineries can sometimes feel a little chilly when it comes to hospitality. Not so at Lynmar. As Anisya says, “We are in the business of joy … making people feel happy and present.” Indeed. Just walking onto the property makes the day’s burdens feel a little lighter.

The 100-acre Russian River Valley estate is lush with vineyards, orchards and bee-friendly gardens filled with flowers, herbs and vegetables. The indoor-outdoor tasting room is designed for maximum “oohs” and “ahhs,” with glorious views in every direction. Indoor seating evokes a fine-dining restaurant, while the patio has a more casual feel. The winery’s seasonal Pinot and Pizza events take place in an intimate redwood grove, with picnic tables and a wood-fired pizza oven.

On the palate

With the many facets of Quail Hill Vineyard, as well as two additional estate vineyards in Forestville and Sebastopol, winemaker Pete Soergel has plenty to work with — even focusing on just two grape varieties.

I didn’t want to stop sipping the 2022 Adam’s Vineyard Russian River Chardonnay ($71), with rich aromas of soft vanilla and bright citrus flavors on the palate. Equally delicious, the silky 2021 Young Vines Russian River Pinot Noir ($69) has cola and spice aromas and concentrated red fruit flavors. Seated tastings cost $60 per person.

Beyond the bottle

If you’re looking for a special experience for, say, an anniversary or birthday, book the Collectors Lunch ($250), overlooking the winery’s organic garden and vineyards.

In-house chef David Frakes creates magical, multicourse menus using estate-grown ingredients, accented with a global spice palette. (I will forever dream of his Thai green curry and coconut soup, studded with garden-fresh peas.) Even the popcorn is remarkable, tossed with toppings like corn-kasundi salt and estate olive oil.

Standard tasting appointments are available at 10 a.m., 12:30 p.m. and 3 p.m. Wednesday through Monday. Lynmar Estate, 3909 Frei Road, Sebastopol, 707-829-3374, lynmarestate.com

Tina Caputo is a wine, food, and travel writer whose work has appeared in numerous publications, including SevenFifty Daily, Visit California, HuffPost, and Sonoma Magazine. Follow Tina on Bluesky @winebroad and view her website at tinacaputo.com.

title: New West Petaluma Home Rich in Hilltop Views, Modern Amenities
summary:
The new home listed for sale in Petaluma features premium interior finishes, a recreation room and multiple patios to take in the views.

The post New West Petaluma Home Rich in Hilltop Views, Modern Amenities appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Among west Petaluma’s concentration of rare, historic homes is a new build for sale in a hilltop cul-de-sac. The five-bedroom, five-bathroom, 5,578-square-foot dwelling is listed at $3,199,999.

The home showcases contemporary style with a low-pitch roof, contrasting exterior sidings and a generous repeat of windows. Premium interior finishes include gray and black stone, geometric marble tiles, dark cabinetry and brass fixtures.

The high-contrast colorless palette, warmed by white oak floors, yields focus to the hilltop views. Glass balcony and staircase railings inside and out add to the minimal aesthetic.

The home sits on nearly 2 acres of sloping property. Multiple patios provide perched gathering spots to take in the views.

The three-story home is rich in amenities: a caterer’s kitchen, Thermador appliances in the main kitchen, a dumbwaiter and a recreation room — pre-wired for a home theater. The garage accommodates five cars.

For more information on 22 Oak Knoll Court in Petaluma, contact listing agent Steven Cozza, 707-328-9766, 707-328-9766, Cozza Team at Compass, 127 Fourth St., Petaluma, compass.com/homedetails/22-Oak-Knoll-Ct-Petaluma-CA-94952/19FB0L_pid/

title: This Forestville Home on the Market Was Built for Entertainment
summary:
Built in 1994 and rooted in traditional style, the home includes a pool, outdoor kitchen, island-style bar, wine cellar and vineyard.

The post This Forestville Home on the Market Was Built for Entertainment appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
A Forestville home, built by the family that lived there for decades, is currently listed for sale. The four-bedroom, three-bathroom home, pool and pool house sit on 3.53 acres. The estate is listed for $4,250,000.

The grounds include a lake with a dock, redwood trees — including a fairy ring grove — and a hand-planted vineyard of Petit Sirah and Sangiovese. Grapes can be processed on the property’s private crush pad and wine processing room. 

The property centers entertainment. Adjacent to the pool and spa is a pool house with an island-style bar and a covered outdoor kitchen, fireplace and bar. 

Built in 1994, the residence is rooted in traditional style with vertical siding, double-hung windows and an iron scroll gate that runs along sections of the rounded wraparound porch. Floors are Douglas fir and cabinets are handmade. A stone-clad wine cellar sits beneath the home and can house up to 90 cases of wine.

The property includes a two-stall equestrian barn that opens up to fenced-in pasture. 

For more information on the property at 6501 Ellen Lane in Forestville, contact listing agent Lisa Sheppard, 707-483-9990, 707-935-2288; Sotheby’s International Realty – Wine Country – Sonoma Brokerage, 793 Broadway, Sonoma, sothebysrealty.com/eng/sales/detail/180-l-1188-2z6kcd/6501-ellen-lane-forestville-ca-95436

title: Día de Los Muertos Celebrations Not To Miss in Sonoma County
summary:
Although Día de los Muertos is traditionally celebrated on Nov. 1 and 2, Sonoma County has a variety of events planned in the coming months.

The post Día de Los Muertos Celebrations Not To Miss in Sonoma County appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Honoring loved ones who’ve gone before through dance, food, music, and gathering with the community is at the heart of Día de los Muertos celebrations all throughout Sonoma County.

Although the holiday is traditionally celebrated on Nov. 1 and 2 in Mexico where it originated, vibrant altars and artwork will be on view at the Museum of Sonoma County for its 30th annual Día de los Muertos exhibit beginning Sept. 5 and running through Nov. 29.

Events during the nearly three month exhibition include a mask-making workshop with artist Maria de Los Angeles on Sept. 6 and a free community block party from noon to 4 p.m. on Saturday, Oct. 10.

title: Take a Hike With Weekly North Bay ‘Go Wild’ Group Excursions
summary:
Santa Rosa's Zoli Somogyi organizes and leads group hikes in Sonoma, Marin, Napa and Lake counties every weekend. Here's how to join — and some of Somogyi's favorite spots to trek.

The post Take a Hike With Weekly North Bay ‘Go Wild’ Group Excursions appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Even though hiking is a solitary diversion, many hikers crave companionship. Enter Go Wild Hikers, which organizes group hikes in Sonoma, Marin, Napa, and Lake counties every weekend of the year.

Executive director Zoli Somogyi of Santa Rosa plots and leads all the hikes himself, sharing his love of the great outdoors with up to 35 friends on any given trip, building community with every step.

“It’s one thing to experience the beauty of Sonoma and Marin counties on your own, but to experience it with other people makes it extra special,” says Somogyi, who has led more than 350 hikes in just over seven years. “The more people participate, the more comfortable they get with themselves, with the outdoors, and with others in the group.”

Most Go Wild hikes average between 4-9 miles, last anywhere from two to six hours, and max out at 1,000-feet gain in elevation. Degrees of difficulty for each hike vary, and participants usually form smaller groups based on strength and skill levels. Some hikes — at least one each month — even accommodate dogs, and all end with an optional post-hike get-together at local pubs and restaurants.

Go Wild suggests a $5 donation each hike, and hikers must cover necessary parking fees at regional and state park outings.

To sign up for a hike, visit the Go Wild page on heylo.com.

Zoli Somogyi’s Favorite Hikes

Pomo Canyon: “From the coast to the canyon, you hike through several different ecosystems. It’s beautiful the whole way.”

Sugarloaf Ridge State Park: “On a clear day, you can see the entire Bay Area from the top of this hike. It makes you realize how close we are to everything else.”

Jack London State Historic Park: “The hike I do there has something for everyone: an orchard, a lake, some redwoods. It packs a lot in.”

Jenner Headlands: “Groups usually say this hike is arduous. I like to think of it as challenging. And spectacular.”

title: DoorDash Names 4 Sonoma County Burger, Hot Dog Spots Among Best in U.S.
summary:
Just in time for Labor Day weekend, here’s where DoorDash reviewers recommend posting up for a great burger or hot dog in Sonoma County.

The post DoorDash Names 4 Sonoma County Burger, Hot Dog Spots Among Best in U.S. appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
DoorDash recently released its top burger and hot dog spots in the U.S. in celebration of Labor Day, with four Sonoma County restaurants making the cut.

The roundup of more than 60 burger joints and hot dog stands stretches from Chicago to Seattle. Among the local favorites recognized by the food-delivery service are Superburger, Acme Burger, Machado Burgers and Ozzie’s Grill.

According to DoorDash, customers used the app to order more than 100 million burgers and 28 million hot dogs last year — a testament to the staying power of two quintessential American foods.

For this year’s roundup, DoorDash analyzed ordering and customer-review data from August 2025 through July 2026. To qualify, restaurants had to be small or medium-sized operations serving burgers and/or hot dogs, with at least 1,000 reviews, fewer than 10 locations and some of the highest average customer ratings.

As Sonoma County heads into the Labor Day weekend, here’s a look at the four local spots DoorDash customers are recommending for a burger or hot dog.

Acme Burger

Originally opened in Cotati in 2019, Acme Burger quickly built a following for its affordable, chef-made burgers. The restaurant has since expanded to five locations across Cotati, Petaluma and Santa Rosa.

The Cotati location has a 4.7-star DoorDash rating from more than 10,000 reviews. Among its highest-rated dishes are the signature Acme Burger, buttermilk fried chicken burger and sweet potato fries.

The freshly ground quarter-pound burgers are seasoned with a signature spice blend and served with crisp lettuce, tomato and house Awesome Sauce on sesame-seed Franco American buns. Acme also serves Miller’s all-beef smoked hot dogs, including a chili cheese dog.

The menu goes well beyond burgers. There are turkey, tuna and veggie burgers; chicken and pulled pork sandwiches; and fried Bodega Bay rock cod. Sides include fries, tater tots, onion rings, fresh salads and scratch-made soups. Milkshakes and ice cream cones are made with Straus chocolate or vanilla soft serve.

Five locations in Cotati, Petaluma and Santa Rosa. acmeburgerco.com

Machado Burgers

With its classic Americana atmosphere, weekly car shows and old-school burger-joint menu, Machado Burgers has long been a Larkfield favorite. The restaurant opened a second location in Windsor last year and serves what is quite possibly the most perfect bacon cheeseburger in Sonoma County.

The Santa Rosa location has a 4.7-star DoorDash rating from more than 2,000 reviews. Its highest-rated dishes include the barbecue bacon cheeseburger, patty melt and regular cheeseburger.

Machado’s burgers are made with 100% ground Angus chuck and topped with cheddar cheese, lettuce, tomato, onion, pickles and house sauce on a seedless bun. The menu also includes turkey and garden burgers, grilled and fried chicken sandwiches, grilled cheeses and tri-tip dips, as well as chicken tenders and corn dogs.

Sides include chili, coleslaw, fries, tater tots and onion rings. For dessert, there are ice cream cones, floats, sundaes, malts and milkshakes.

406 Larkfield Center, Santa Rosa, 707-546-6835; 9238 Old Redwood Highway, Suite 126, Windsor, 707-620-0258. machadoburgers.com

Ozzie’s Grill

Ozzie’s Grill has been serving Santa Rosa since 1992, earning a following for its oversized burgers and old-school atmosphere.

On DoorDash, Ozzie’s Grill has a 4.7-star rating from more than 3,000 reviews. Its highest-rated items include the bacon cheeseburger, corn dogs and milkshakes.

The freshly ground beef burgers come with a choice of cheese and toppings, including lettuce, tomato, onion, pickles and mayonnaise, all served on a soft bun. The menu also includes veggie and turkey burgers, assorted sandwiches, hot dogs and corn dogs, chicken tenders and fish and chips.

Sides include salads, fries, onion rings and housemade chili. Dessert options range from milkshakes and ice cream cones to banana splits, hot fudge sundaes and root beer floats.

799 Montecito Center, Santa Rosa, 707-538-0775. sites.google.com/bmaac.com/ozzies-grill

Superburger

Superburger traces its roots to the 1950s, when it opened in a small shack off Fourth Street in Santa Rosa. The longtime local institution still serves old-fashioned, char-grilled burgers from its original Fourth Street location, along with a second location in Cotati.

Over the years, Superburger expanded to locations in Cotati, Petaluma, Penngrove, Santa Rosa and Windsor. Most have since closed as the owner has returned the business to its roots.

The original Santa Rosa location has a 4.6-star DoorDash rating from more than 6,000 reviews. Its highest-rated items include beer-battered onion rings, the bacon-and-cheese Superburger and milkshakes.

The third-pound Black Angus burgers are char-grilled and served with a choice of cheese, lettuce, onion, tomato and pickles, plus Supersauce on soft potato buns. Superburger also serves third-pound, all-beef kosher hot dogs, including chili and Reuben dogs.

Beyond its burgers, the menu includes charbroiled chicken sandwiches, French dips and a sourdough patty melt. Sides include fries, tater tots, onion rings and pineapple coleslaw. There are also fresh-brewed iced teas and lemonades, along with more than 20 milkshake flavors.

1501 Fourth St., Santa Rosa, 707-546-4016; 8204 Old Redwood Highway, Cotati, 707-665-9790. originalsuperburger.com

title: Where to Celebrate Rosh Hashanah in Sonoma County
summary:
Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year, will be observed from Sept. 11-13. These Sonoma County spots are celebrating with traditional services and dinners.

The post Where to Celebrate Rosh Hashanah in Sonoma County appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Rosh Hashanah, the two-day Jewish New Year, is celebrated with feasts, prayer, candle lighting and blowing the shofar, a ram’s horn. This year, the holiday begins at sundown on Friday, Sept. 11, and continues through nightfall Sunday, Sept. 13.

Traditional foods served during Rosh Hashanah include challah, dates, pomegranates and apples dipped in honey, all meant to symbolize a sweet year ahead. Fish — particularly a fish head or the head of another kosher animal — is also customary, representing the biblical wish “that we be a head and not a tail.” Tzimmes, a traditional Jewish dish made with carrots or other root vegetables, is associated with prosperity; the Yiddish word for carrots, meren, means “to multiply.”

Sonoma County restaurants and Jewish congregations will celebrate Rosh Hashanah with a variety of dinners, services and family programs, blending traditional observances with a Wine Country touch. Shanah tovah!

Celebrations

Congregation Shomrei Torah

Santa Rosa’s Congregation Shomrei Torah will hold several services and a potluck for Rosh Hashanah. A children’s service will be held from 5-6 p.m. on Sept. 11, followed by a full Erev Rosh Hashanah service from 7:30-9 p.m., featuring prayer and song, at the Center For Spiritual Living (2075 Occidental Road). A morning service will be held from 10:30 a.m. to 1 p.m. Sept. 12 at the same location. Youth programs for ages 2-18 will be available.

The congregation will hold a Tashlich service from 4-5 p.m. Sept. 12 at Lake Ralphine in Howarth Park (630 Summerfield Road, Santa Rosa). A second-day Rosh Hashanah service and potluck will be held from 10:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. Sept. 13 at Congregation Shomrei Torah.

The events are free, but registration is required. Learn more and register online. Congregation Shomrei Torah, 2600 Bennett Valley Road, Santa Rosa, 707-578-5519, cstsr.org

Joseph Weingarten Chabad Jewish Center

Santa Rosa’s Joseph Weingarten Chabad Jewish Center will host evening Rosh Hashanah services followed by a dinner at 7 p.m. Sept. 11.

Services and lunch will be held at 10 a.m. Sept. 12 and 13, with a Rosh Hashanah children’s program at 11 a.m. Sept. 12.

There is no charge for the dinner or services, but donations are appreciated. RSVP or donate online. Joseph Weingarten Chabad Jewish Center, 2461 Summerfield Road, Santa Rosa, 707-577-0277, jewishsonoma.com

Congregation Beth Ami

Congregation Beth Ami will host Rabbi Ron Koas and cantorial soloist Jessie Leider for an Erev Rosh Hashanah service, 7:30-8:30 p.m. Sept. 11 followed by an oneg, or after-service social gathering, with sparkling wine, apple cider and honey cake.

The congregation will hold a Tashlich service and community potluck on the second day of Rosh Hashanah. The service begins at 4:30 p.m. Sept. 13 at Lake Ralphine in Howarth Park.

A vegetarian potluck starts at 6 p.m. at Congregation Beth Ami, followed by a ma’ariv prayer service at 7 p.m. in the Beth Ami Sanctuary. Guests may bring a dairy or vegetarian dish to share and a drink of their choice.

RSVP to the Beth Ami office by noon Sept. 10. Congregation Beth Ami, 4676 Mayette Ave., Santa Rosa, 707-360-3000, bethamisr.org

Congregation Ner Shalom

Cotati’s Congregation Ner Shalom will celebrate the High Holy Days with a weekend of Rosh Hashanah services. The congregation will welcome the new year at 7 p.m. Sept. 11 with prayer and music from the Good Shabbos Band and the Ner Shalom Singers.

There will be a Rosh Hashanah family service with song, prayer, a play and children’s activities at 9 a.m. Sept. 12 at the Ner Shalom courtyard. The family service is free to attend but requires registration; register online. The family service will be followed by a traditional Rosh Hashanah morning service at 10:15 a.m. led by Rabbi Irwin Keller, held in person and in the “High Holy Day Zoom Room.” A picnic lunch and tashlikh ritual will take place at 1:30 p.m. Sept. 12 on the courtyard. Guests can bring their own lunch and Ner Shalom will provide challah, beverages, and apples and honey.

Ner Shalom will close out the Rosh Hashanah celebration with a collage workshop at 11 a.m. Sept. 13 in which guests will create two collage cards to serve as personal touchstones.

Learn more about Rosh Hashanah services and register for events online. Congregation Ner Shalom, 85 La Plaza, Cotati, 707-664-8622, nershalom.org

Chabad Jewish Center of Petaluma

Petaluma’s Chabad Jewish Center will host a traditional Rosh Hashanah community dinner at 6:30 p.m. Sept. 11 at the Chabad center on Keller Street. The dinner will include round challah, apples and honey, brisket and more. Tickets are $40 for adults and $20 for children. Holiday services and shofar blowing will be held at the center from 10:30 a.m. to noon Sept. 13. A Rosh Hashanah Kids Fest, with crafts, games, sweet treats and a beekeeper demonstration, will be held from 4-5 p.m. Sept. 13 at Lucchesi Park. The festival will be followed by shofar blowing and a Tashlich meditation at 5 p.m.

There is no charge for the Sept. 13 services, though donations are appreciated. RSVP or purchase dinner tickets online. Chabad Jewish Center of Petaluma, 205 Keller St., Petaluma, 707-559-8585, jewishpetaluma.com

B’nai Israel Center for Jewish Life

Petaluma’s B’nai Israel Center for Jewish Life will celebrate Rosh Hashanah with a weekend of services, music, luncheons and more. For Erev Rosh Hashanah, the Center will host an oneg, a Shabbat ritual, in the backyard at 5 p.m. and a musical service at 6 p.m. Sept. 11.

On Sept. 12, there will be a Torah study at 9 a.m. followed by a traditional holiday service at 9:3o a.m., and a Kiddush lunch will be held at 12:30 p.m.

On Sept. 13, the center will serve coffee and doughnuts from 9-10 a.m. — including a pre-service meditation from 9:15-9:45 a.m. — followed by a Rosh Hashanah service with shofar from 10 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. Guests are welcome to join the center for a BYO picnic at 4 p.m. at Petaluma River Park (100 E. D St.). A family service will be held at 5 p.m. followed by a Tashlich service at 5:30 p.m. at the park. All ages are welcome.

Learn more and RSVP for services online. B’nai Israel Center for Jewish Life, 740 Western Ave., Petaluma, 707-762-0340, petalumajewishlife.org

Congregation Shir Shalom

Sonoma’s Congregation Shir Shalom will host Rosh Hashanah evening services at 6:30 p.m. Sept. 11 and morning services at 9 a.m. Sept. 12. The holiday celebration will include a Rosh Hashanah luncheon and Tashlich service starting at 1:15 p.m. Sept. 12 on the Sonoma Plaza. Boxed lunches will be available in the community room.

Tickets for Rosh Hashanah and/or Yom Kippur services range from $72-$144; purchase online. Congregation Shir Shalom, 252 W. Spain St., Sonoma, 707-935-3636, shir-shalom.org

Sonoma Valley Chabad Jewish Center

The Sonoma Valley Chabad Jewish Center will host a dinner, prayer services and other programs during Rosh Hashanah. A community dinner will be held at 6:30 p.m. Sept. 11 at the Sonoma Valley Woman’s Club (574 First St. E.). Dinner is $54 per person; purchase tickets online.

On Sept. 12 and 13, the Chabad center will host morning prayer services at 10 a.m., a children’s program at 11 a.m. and lunch buffet at noon at 430 W. Napa St., Suite F, in Sonoma. The Rosh Hashanah gathering will include shofar blowing at 11:30 a.m. Sept. 13.

A separate shofar blowing and Tashlich meditation will take place at 5 p.m. Sept. 13 on the Sonoma Plaza.

Holiday services Sept. 12-13 are free and open to all. RSVP or make a donation online. Sonoma Valley Chabad Jewish Center, 858 Third St. W., Sonoma, 929-253-0820, svjewishcenter.com/highholidays

Food

Drewish Deli

Healdsburg’s traditional Jewish deli and bagel shop is offering High Holiday catering for Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. The menu, available as a full meal or a la carte, includes round plain or raisin challah; potato latkes with applesauce and creme fraiche; matzo ball soup; brisket with gravy and horseradish aioli; chocolate or cinnamon babka; and chocolate or cinnamon-apple butter rugelach. Order by Sept. 6 for Rosh Hashanah and by Sept. 15 for Yom Kippur.

Orders can be placed online, by phone or in person at the deli. 11 Mitchell Lane, Healdsburg, 707-955-0600, drewishdeli.com

Grossman’s Noshery & Bar

Jewish deli and restaurant Grossman’s will offer a Rosh Hashanah menu for dine-in, pickup and delivery Sept. 11-13.

The menu includes round challah with raisins and currants; potato-leek latkes with applesauce and sour cream; pomegranate-molasses roasted carrots; a smoked and pickled fish board; and honey cake with apple buttercream, along with other Grossman’s staples. Preorders are available now; order online. 308 Wilson St., Santa Rosa, 707-595-7707, grossmanssr.com

Marla Bakery

Marla will offer round raisin challah with honey for pickup Sept. 11-13 at its downtown Santa Rosa bakery and at select Bay Area farmers markets. $15 each. Order online for pickup. 208 Davis St., Santa Rosa, 707-852-4098, marlabakery.com

Sonoma Wine Shop & La Bodega

Sebastopol’s La Bodega will celebrate Rosh Hashanah with a social hour beginning at 5 p.m. and dinner service at 6 p.m. Sept. 13. Jewish musician and educator Rick Concoff will lead a holiday service in song at 5:30 p.m., with traditional apples and honey available for snacking.

The dinner menu includes raisin challah; apple and endive salad with pomegranate; saffron and rose petal arancini; Jerusalem kugel; tzimmes, or orange-glazed carrots; Middle Eastern stuffed cabbage; honey date cake; and apple tarts.

Dinner is $69 for adult guests, $59 for members, $49 for youth ages 13-17, $39 for children ages 6-12 and $29 for kids ages 2-5. Learn more and purchase tickets online. 2295 Gravenstein Highway S., Sebastopol, 707-827-1832, sonomawineshop.com

title: Graton Finally Gets Its Coffee Shop and Much More
summary:
Graton Station, a new cafe and bakery in a former firehouse, aims to bring coffee, local food and community to the heart of town.

The post Graton Finally Gets Its Coffee Shop and Much More appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
The close-knit community of Graton is missing something most of us take for granted: a coffee shop. Not a restaurant, but a place to run into neighbors over a latte, bring the kids, linger with the dog or sit at a table with nowhere else to be.

That is the idea behind Graton Station, a new cafe and bakery being created in the heart of town by Ferrell Carter, Adrian Apana, Tori Immel and Matt Jorgensen, four locals with a shared goal.

This summer, the group opened the first phase of the project: a weekend coffee cart outside the former Graton firehouse, serving from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m. Saturdays and Sundays. The building has sat mostly empty for nearly 13 years. Now, behind the espresso machine and patio tables, construction is underway on its next life: a full cafe and bakery with communal tables, lounge space and room for dinners, music and other gatherings.

But the coffee shop is only part of the plan.

Fine-dining chefs, communal thinking

For Immel, the project is rooted in a broader question: What makes a town feel alive? Her answer has less to do with grand attractions than with the ordinary places where people can linger, talk and get to know one another.

She and Jorgensen have been pursuing that idea through ReVillage Foundation, the nonprofit they co-founded to strengthen Graton’s local economy and create more shared community spaces. The nearby Graton Town Square is another piece of that effort, connecting Graton Station to a larger attempt to make the center of town more active and welcoming.

That vision appealed to Carter and Apana, who were looking for a way to take what they had learned in ambitious restaurant kitchens and apply it to something more everyday — and more communal.

The two chefs have worked at restaurants and bakeries including SingleThread, Troubadour Bread & Bistro, Quail & Condor and Maison Porcella. But they were not interested in opening another destination restaurant where the price and formality might put it out of reach for the people who live nearby.

Instead, they launched Preservatory, a food preservation and reclamation project that eventually brought them together with Immel and Jorgensen.

The connection was natural. ReVillage was looking for ways to strengthen Graton’s town center. Carter and Apana wanted to make the traditions of local food and preservation part of everyday life.

The common ground was simple: Bring Graton to the table.

Good food, good vibes

As Graton Station grows, its menu will move beyond coffee and pastries to breakfast and lunch, changing with the seasons and whatever local farms and producers have in abundance.

The early ideas include breakfast sandwiches, savory porridge, mushroom toast, soups, salads and roasted chicken sandwiches, alongside housemade breads and pastries.

That “of the moment” approach is central to Preservatory.

Carter and Apana are interested in extending the life of Sonoma County’s abundance — apples, tomatoes, berries and other produce — by turning it into jams, pickles, sauces, shrubs and other pantry staples. Instead of disappearing when the season ends, the harvest can reappear months later.

At the weekend coffee cart, their shrubs are already being served as refreshing sodas.

The chefs also want to revive some of the kitchen knowledge that has largely disappeared from home cooking: canning, fermenting and other forms of preservation. Classes and demonstrations are planned for the future.

Another idea in the works is a community-supported kitchen, loosely modeled on a community-supported agriculture program. Members would receive a rotating selection of baked goods, prepared foods and pantry items based on what local farms have in abundance.

For now, the Graton Station team has packed an ambitious list of ideas into a small former firehouse: local food, preservation, shared knowledge, community ownership and a more active town center.

But at its heart, it’s a simple recipe: Graton needed a coffee shop, with some cake and conversation to go with it.

Graton Station is raising money through Wefunder, allowing community members to invest directly in the project.

title: Best Soft Serve in Sonoma County: 9 Places To Try
summary:
Our dining editor spent the summer tasting Sonoma County’s soft serve, from creamy classics and chocolate-dipped cones to chef-driven desserts and over-the-top toppings. Here are the favorites.

The post Best Soft Serve in Sonoma County: 9 Places To Try appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
You can learn a lot about soft serve by taste-testing nearly every cone in the county. I did exactly that this summer.

First, not all soft serve is created equal. Some is thicker, some airier, some icier; even when two places use the same base, the results can be radically different. Second, Sonoma County’s dairies make some very good soft serve. And finally, I have yet to meet a twist cone I didn’t fall at least a little bit in love with.

Most of Sonoma County’s soft-serve machines use a liquid base from either Straus Family Creamery or Valley Ford Creamery. We’re more than a little spoiled to have either: Both make exceptional dairy.

This list is strictly about dairy soft serve. No yogurt, sorbet, custard or anything else that comes out of a machine and requires its own category. So don’t come at me with your little plastic spoons.

Here are the results of my very unscientific tour of Sonoma County’s soft-serve scene.

Absolute Best Soft Serve: Valley Ford Creamery

The highest praise I can give a dessert is “last-meal good,” and this velvety, butterfat-rich soft serve qualifies. Valley Ford Creamery uses milk from its own Jersey cows to make gelato-smooth vanilla and chocolate soft serve at its cafe and cheese-aging facility. The herd’s high-fat milk gives the frozen dessert a texture that is dense, silky and remarkably easy to keep eating. You may be ruined for lesser soft serve.

14390 Valley Ford Road, Valley Ford, 707-875-7073, valleyfordcheese.com

Most Interesting Toppings: Altamont General Store

Grilled pickled pineapple may be the strangest soft-serve topping on this list, but don’t dismiss it before you try it. Its sweet-tart acidity is excellent with creamy vanilla. Try the Pineapple Express, with organic soft serve, grilled pickled pineapple, passion fruit syrup and sea salt. Other toppings include olive oil, vegan chocolate cookies and gluten-free tahini brownie.

While you’re there, don’t miss the Umami Cloud: miso caramel cold foam dusted with caramel salt over iced chai. Chef’s kiss.

3703 Main St., Occidental, 707-874-6053, altamontgeneralstore.com

Most Committed: Valley Swim Club

Valley Swim Club takes its soft serve seriously. This isn’t a dessert tacked onto the menu; it’s a pillar of the casual, seafood-centric operation. If you’re a cone person, rainbow sprinkles, cookie crumbles, toasted peanuts and white chocolate chips are good choices. Sea salt and olive oil, caramel and chocolate sauce are better contained in a cup. But you do you. The soft serve also makes an excellent shake.

18709 Arnold Drive, Sonoma, 707-243-3032, valleyswim.club

Best Float: River Electric

Of course you’ll want a root beer float while lounging by the pool. Creamy vanilla soft serve and Boylan’s not-too-sweet root beer make an ideal summer combination. Add a shot of bourbon, and you have a relaxation strategy, even with a million kids screaming nearby.

16101 Neeley Road, Guerneville, 707-937-8915, theriverelectric.com

Best for Dip Cones: Foster’s Freeze

Don’t ask what makes that perfect chocolate shell around soft serve so good. You probably don’t want to know. Just order the dip cone and remember childhood: those blistering summer days when Mom and Dad drove to Foster’s Freeze to keep you and your siblings occupied for a while. Oh, the good old days. Even as an adult, accept that some chocolate will probably end up on your shirt. And your shoes. That’s part of the experience.

855 Sebastopol Road, Santa Rosa; 1400 Fourth St., Santa Rosa. fostersfreeze.com

Most Cheffy: Dead Letter

The newish Sonoma restaurant takes soft serve into fine-dining territory, finishing its vanilla swirl with dark-chocolate hard shell and sesame-honeycomb candy. It’s fancy without taking itself too seriously, with plenty of nods to childhood.

101 E. Napa St., Sonoma, 707-933-3665, deadlettersonoma.com

Best Twist: Handline

I have a suspicious number of $7.13 charges from Handline on my credit-card statement this summer. They’re all for the same thing: a large chocolate-and-vanilla twist from the soft-serve window. Those brown-and-white swirls became my post-kayaking reward, hot-day cool-down and “I made it through Monday” consolation. Worth every cent. Usually eaten in my car.

935 Gravenstein Highway S., Sebastopol, 707-827-3744, handline.com

Best Olive Oil: Bravas Bar de Tapas

Delicate tangerine olive oil is a surprising topping to the velvety vanilla soft serve, the savory-sweet combo tastes like the fanciest creamsicle you’ve ever had. If you’re a sweet-on-sweet person, the deep cajeta-style caramel topping takes burnt-sugar sweetness to another level. 420 Center St., Healdsburg, 707-433-7700, barbravas.com

Best Brittle: Grossman’s

Grossman’s serves soft serve with its own collection of toppings, including candied strawberries, white-chocolate crumble, Bubbies brittle and tahini caramel. 308 Wilson St., Santa Rosa, 707-595-7707, grossmanssr.com

Best Affogato: Diavola Pizzeria & Salumeria

A shot of hot espresso poured over cold soft serve is perhaps the best argument for dessert after lunch. The combination of melting soft serve and strong coffee is hard to resist, particularly when you need an afternoon pick-me-up. Eat it with a spoon, then drink whatever’s left.

21021 Geyserville Ave., Geyserville, 707-814-0111, diavolapizzeria.com

How soft-serve machines work

Eating this much soft serve means eventually getting into the mechanics of the machine, because a few settings can mean the difference between an icy mess and a dense, creamy swirl.

Soft serve begins as a liquid mix that is chilled, churned and aerated inside the machine. As the mix freezes, a scraper sweeps it out of the freezing chamber while incorporating air, a process known as “overrun.” That air is a big part of what gives soft serve its characteristic texture.

Most commercial soft-serve machines target an overrun of roughly 30% to 60%. In other words, a gallon of liquid mix can produce about 1.3 to 1.6 gallons of soft serve.

Machines can be calibrated for different temperatures, consistencies and amounts of air. More air produces a lighter, fluffier swirl; less produces something denser and richer.

The mix itself matters, too. Fat and sugar affect how the base freezes and melts, which helps explain why two shops using the same dairy mix can produce noticeably different results. One may hold a tall, firm twist; another may be softer and silkier.

title: New Sonoma County Restaurants To Eat at Right Now
summary:
More than a dozen new restaurants have opened or are on the way in Sonoma County. Here’s where to eat now and what to keep an eye on.

The post New Sonoma County Restaurants To Eat at Right Now appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Keeping up with Sonoma County’s restaurant scene is a full-time job, and this summer I’ve been racing from Healdsburg and Sebastopol to Sonoma and Santa Rosa to try to keep pace. More than a dozen new restaurants have opened in recent weeks, with more on the way. That’s a lot of new menus to work through. Here’s what’s open, what’s coming and where you might want to make your next reservation.

Now open

Dead Letter

The latest restaurant from the team behind the girl & the fig brings a dose of drama to Sonoma’s 19th-century post office, just off the plaza. A Spanish charcoal grill anchors a menu that moves from chicken karaage with hummus to butterflied trout with red curry, with plenty of dishes designed for sharing. The dim, art-filled dining room has a postal-noir sensibility, with surreal digital screens, vintage touches and even a $5 Art-o-mat vending machine. Dinner, apparently, can come with a little diversion. 101 E. Napa St., Sonoma, deadlettersonoma.com

Café Carrusel

Owner Ivy Reyes has turned childhood dreams of an Easy-Bake Oven, clouds of glitter and carousel horses into a Mexi-brunch cafe that makes Barbie’s Dreamhouse look restrained. The six-page menu mixes American and Latin flavors with carnival theatrics: consommé-soaked birria tacos hang from a clothesline; a butterfly-shaped brunch board arrives with pancakes, waffles, French toast and Nutella; and cocktails are topped with fluffy pink cotton candy. This is food designed for fun rather than fine dining, with plenty of glazes, marshmallows and chocolate. Because everyone deserves a little glitter-topped make-believe. 630 Third St., Santa Rosa, 707-655-8365, instagram.com/cafe_carrusel

Capriciano Osteria

Sonoma County has no shortage of Italian restaurants, so a new one needs to give diners a reason to add another to the list. Capriciano Osteria has found one in chef Baki Bekci, whose background includes Four Seasons kitchens and the founding of Mezzaluna. He brings a fine-dining sensibility to Italian-American staples, from warm focaccia and burrata salad to fresh pasta, chicken Parmesan and risotto. Among the standouts are lemon ravioli, grilled octopus and a seafood risotto loaded with shrimp, lobster and clams. 505 Mendocino Ave., Santa Rosa, 707-800-7904, capriciano.com

Dolce Rosa Cafe

I’m not here to defend $20 avocado toast. But if you’re going to spend $20 on it, Santa Rosa’s Dolce Rosa Cafe makes a persuasive case. The all-day cafe gives familiar dishes a fine-dining gloss, from housemade focaccia piled with avocado, burrata, pistachios and hot honey to tiramisu pancakes with espresso mascarpone. A pistachio latte comes rimmed with crushed nuts. Owners Josie Ortega and Martin Chaparro are still tinkering with the menu, which also includes pastas, breakfast burritos and eggs in purgatory. Dinner service may be coming later. 4910 Sonoma Highway, Suite B, Santa Rosa, 707-931-4625, instagram.com/dolcerosacafe

Spur Saloon

Batwing doors, saddle seats, cocktails and 10-gallon-hat fun: Spur Saloon is Windsor’s new country-Western bar. More details are coming next week. 9000 Windsor Road, Windsor, instagram.com/spur.saloon.windsor

Bonnie Bagels & Co.

A small Sebastopol cafe may have finally cracked the code on East Coast bagels in Sonoma County. Bonnie Bagels opened in mid-August with kettle-cooked bagels — boiled and baked, as they should be — that are crisp on the outside, chewy on the inside, and, best of all, available in salt. Owner Michael Sousa and executive chef Greg Kalergis offer the familiar lineup of bagels, schmears, and sandwiches, along with more California-leaning flavors like cheddar-jalapeño and Asiago. The shop occupies the former Hippizzazz pizza space across from HopMonk. 280 S. Main St., Sebastopol, 707-503-6520, bonniebagels.com

The Porch

Chef Lisa Boisset is obsessive about making nearly everything at her tiny Sebastopol bistro from scratch, from stocks and sauces to dressings and focaccia croutons. Even the ketchup gets a multistep treatment: tomatoes are charred, then combined with warm spices, apple cider vinegar and balsamic vinegar. The result makes the Parmesan- and parsley-topped pommes frites particularly difficult to share. Tucked beside Patisserie Angelica and behind the Rialto Cinemas, the modest brasserie serves straightforward, comforting food without much fuss. Its west county porch feels more like a roadhouse than the Parisian Left Bank. 6811 Laguna Park Way, Sebastopol, 707-393-9488, theporchkitchen.com

Wylde Provisions Co.

At this Sebastopol playground cafe, parents can sit in the shade with a proper espresso — or a beer — and a chef-made tofu soba noodle bowl while their children run wild. The menu ranges from yogurt parfaits with blueberry sauce to a giant carnitas sandwich with refried lentils and tomatillo-fish-sauce vinaigrette. But bowls are the specialty, with new combinations appearing weekly. Recent options include the Tamariana Grande, with tamari-glazed turkey sausage over udon with edamame, charred zucchini, pickled ginger and cashew-tamari vinaigrette, and the Chipotle Off the Old Block, with chipotle chicken or tofu, quinoa, black beans, corn and greens in avocado-cilantro dressing. Good food, even if you’re not chasing a toddler. 500 Robinson Road, Sebastopol, instagram.com/wyldeprovisionsco

Hazel

Sometimes when one door closes, another opens — in this case, a 150-year-old yellow clapboard Victorian overlooking downtown Occidental. Less than a year after closing their original location, owners Jim and Michele Wimborough have reopened their decade-old restaurant in the former Barley & Hops space down the street. The airy dining room, with its 19th-century details and tucked-away nooks, already feels like a neighborhood gathering place. The menu remains recognizably Hazel, with wood-fired pizzas, hearty seasonal dishes and the unfussy hospitality that has made the restaurant a west county favorite. 3688 Bohemian Highway, Occidental, 707-874-6003, restauranthazel.com

Also on the radar

title: Lynmar Estate Is a Lush Garden Retreat Minutes From Sebastopol
summary:
The Russian River winery tempts visitors with elegant Pinot Noir and Chardonnay alongside flower-filled gardens.

The post Lynmar Estate Is a Lush Garden Retreat Minutes From Sebastopol appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
There’s no hustle or bustle at Lynmar Estate. Set just a few miles from downtown Sebastopol, the Russian River Valley winery has a knack for whisking visitors away from everyday life with natural beauty and warm hospitality.

The story

San Francisco native Lynn Fritz spent his childhood summers on the Russian River. In 1980, as the founder of a global logistics company, he bought Quail Hill Vineyard near Sebastopol as a family retreat.

The Russian River Valley property came with 30 acres of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay vineyards, which officially made Fritz a grape grower. Winemakers Merry Edwards, then working at Matanzas Creek, and Tony Soter, at Etude, were among his early clients.

Fritz had no intention of starting a winery of his own, but perhaps the story of the estate’s original owner had a subtle influence: Gold Rush prospector Lewis Meyer made the first wine at the site in the 1880s. With the help of winemaker Daniel Moore, Lynmar Estate produced its inaugural vintage in 1994.

Fritz and his wife, Anisya, made Quail Hill Vineyard their permanent home in 2008, and together they now run the day-to-day operations of the winery and tasting room. Over the years, Quail Hill’s Pinot Noir and Chardonnay plantings have expanded to 44 acres, all certified organic. The winery produces about 10,000 cases a year.

Wine isn’t the couple’s only passion. In 2001, after Lynn sold his logistics company to UPS, the couple co-founded the Fritz Institute, a nonprofit logistics organization that helps deliver relief supplies to disaster-stricken communities around the world.

The vibe

Higher-end wineries can sometimes feel a little chilly when it comes to hospitality. Not so at Lynmar. As Anisya says, “We are in the business of joy … making people feel happy and present.” Indeed. Just walking onto the property makes the day’s burdens feel a little lighter.

The 100-acre Russian River Valley estate is lush with vineyards, orchards and bee-friendly gardens filled with flowers, herbs and vegetables. The indoor-outdoor tasting room is designed for maximum “oohs” and “ahhs,” with glorious views in every direction. Indoor seating evokes a fine-dining restaurant, while the patio has a more casual feel. The winery’s seasonal Pinot and Pizza events take place in an intimate redwood grove, with picnic tables and a wood-fired pizza oven.

On the palate

With the many facets of Quail Hill Vineyard, as well as two additional estate vineyards in Forestville and Sebastopol, winemaker Pete Soergel has plenty to work with — even focusing on just two grape varieties.

I didn’t want to stop sipping the 2022 Adam’s Vineyard Russian River Chardonnay ($71), with rich aromas of soft vanilla and bright citrus flavors on the palate. Equally delicious, the silky 2021 Young Vines Russian River Pinot Noir ($69) has cola and spice aromas and concentrated red fruit flavors. Seated tastings cost $60 per person.

Beyond the bottle

If you’re looking for a special experience for, say, an anniversary or birthday, book the Collectors Lunch ($250), overlooking the winery’s organic garden and vineyards.

In-house chef David Frakes creates magical, multicourse menus using estate-grown ingredients, accented with a global spice palette. (I will forever dream of his Thai green curry and coconut soup, studded with garden-fresh peas.) Even the popcorn is remarkable, tossed with toppings like corn-kasundi salt and estate olive oil.

Standard tasting appointments are available at 10 a.m., 12:30 p.m. and 3 p.m. Wednesday through Monday. Lynmar Estate, 3909 Frei Road, Sebastopol, 707-829-3374, lynmarestate.com

Tina Caputo is a wine, food, and travel writer whose work has appeared in numerous publications, including SevenFifty Daily, Visit California, HuffPost, and Sonoma Magazine. Follow Tina on Bluesky @winebroad and view her website at tinacaputo.com.

title: Take a Hike With Weekly North Bay ‘Go Wild’ Group Excursions
summary:
Santa Rosa's Zoli Somogyi organizes and leads group hikes in Sonoma, Marin, Napa and Lake counties every weekend. Here's how to join — and some of Somogyi's favorite spots to trek.

The post Take a Hike With Weekly North Bay ‘Go Wild’ Group Excursions appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Even though hiking is a solitary diversion, many hikers crave companionship. Enter Go Wild Hikers, which organizes group hikes in Sonoma, Marin, Napa, and Lake counties every weekend of the year.

Executive director Zoli Somogyi of Santa Rosa plots and leads all the hikes himself, sharing his love of the great outdoors with up to 35 friends on any given trip, building community with every step.

“It’s one thing to experience the beauty of Sonoma and Marin counties on your own, but to experience it with other people makes it extra special,” says Somogyi, who has led more than 350 hikes in just over seven years. “The more people participate, the more comfortable they get with themselves, with the outdoors, and with others in the group.”

Most Go Wild hikes average between 4-9 miles, last anywhere from two to six hours, and max out at 1,000-feet gain in elevation. Degrees of difficulty for each hike vary, and participants usually form smaller groups based on strength and skill levels. Some hikes — at least one each month — even accommodate dogs, and all end with an optional post-hike get-together at local pubs and restaurants.

Go Wild suggests a $5 donation each hike, and hikers must cover necessary parking fees at regional and state park outings.

To sign up for a hike, visit the Go Wild page on heylo.com.

Zoli Somogyi’s Favorite Hikes

Pomo Canyon: “From the coast to the canyon, you hike through several different ecosystems. It’s beautiful the whole way.”

Sugarloaf Ridge State Park: “On a clear day, you can see the entire Bay Area from the top of this hike. It makes you realize how close we are to everything else.”

Jack London State Historic Park: “The hike I do there has something for everyone: an orchard, a lake, some redwoods. It packs a lot in.”

Jenner Headlands: “Groups usually say this hike is arduous. I like to think of it as challenging. And spectacular.”

title: DoorDash Names 4 Sonoma County Burger, Hot Dog Spots Among Best in U.S.
summary:
Just in time for Labor Day weekend, here’s where DoorDash reviewers recommend posting up for a great burger or hot dog in Sonoma County.

The post DoorDash Names 4 Sonoma County Burger, Hot Dog Spots Among Best in U.S. appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
DoorDash recently released its top burger and hot dog spots in the U.S. in celebration of Labor Day, with four Sonoma County restaurants making the cut.

The roundup of more than 60 burger joints and hot dog stands stretches from Chicago to Seattle. Among the local favorites recognized by the food-delivery service are Superburger, Acme Burger, Machado Burgers and Ozzie’s Grill.

According to DoorDash, customers used the app to order more than 100 million burgers and 28 million hot dogs last year — a testament to the staying power of two quintessential American foods.

For this year’s roundup, DoorDash analyzed ordering and customer-review data from August 2025 through July 2026. To qualify, restaurants had to be small or medium-sized operations serving burgers and/or hot dogs, with at least 1,000 reviews, fewer than 10 locations and some of the highest average customer ratings.

As Sonoma County heads into the Labor Day weekend, here’s a look at the four local spots DoorDash customers are recommending for a burger or hot dog.

Acme Burger

Originally opened in Cotati in 2019, Acme Burger quickly built a following for its affordable, chef-made burgers. The restaurant has since expanded to five locations across Cotati, Petaluma and Santa Rosa.

The Cotati location has a 4.7-star DoorDash rating from more than 10,000 reviews. Among its highest-rated dishes are the signature Acme Burger, buttermilk fried chicken burger and sweet potato fries.

The freshly ground quarter-pound burgers are seasoned with a signature spice blend and served with crisp lettuce, tomato and house Awesome Sauce on sesame-seed Franco American buns. Acme also serves Miller’s all-beef smoked hot dogs, including a chili cheese dog.

The menu goes well beyond burgers. There are turkey, tuna and veggie burgers; chicken and pulled pork sandwiches; and fried Bodega Bay rock cod. Sides include fries, tater tots, onion rings, fresh salads and scratch-made soups. Milkshakes and ice cream cones are made with Straus chocolate or vanilla soft serve.

Five locations in Cotati, Petaluma and Santa Rosa. acmeburgerco.com

Machado Burgers

With its classic Americana atmosphere, weekly car shows and old-school burger-joint menu, Machado Burgers has long been a Larkfield favorite. The restaurant opened a second location in Windsor last year and serves what is quite possibly the most perfect bacon cheeseburger in Sonoma County.

The Santa Rosa location has a 4.7-star DoorDash rating from more than 2,000 reviews. Its highest-rated dishes include the barbecue bacon cheeseburger, patty melt and regular cheeseburger.

Machado’s burgers are made with 100% ground Angus chuck and topped with cheddar cheese, lettuce, tomato, onion, pickles and house sauce on a seedless bun. The menu also includes turkey and garden burgers, grilled and fried chicken sandwiches, grilled cheeses and tri-tip dips, as well as chicken tenders and corn dogs.

Sides include chili, coleslaw, fries, tater tots and onion rings. For dessert, there are ice cream cones, floats, sundaes, malts and milkshakes.

406 Larkfield Center, Santa Rosa, 707-546-6835; 9238 Old Redwood Highway, Suite 126, Windsor, 707-620-0258. machadoburgers.com

Ozzie’s Grill

Ozzie’s Grill has been serving Santa Rosa since 1992, earning a following for its oversized burgers and old-school atmosphere.

On DoorDash, Ozzie’s Grill has a 4.7-star rating from more than 3,000 reviews. Its highest-rated items include the bacon cheeseburger, corn dogs and milkshakes.

The freshly ground beef burgers come with a choice of cheese and toppings, including lettuce, tomato, onion, pickles and mayonnaise, all served on a soft bun. The menu also includes veggie and turkey burgers, assorted sandwiches, hot dogs and corn dogs, chicken tenders and fish and chips.

Sides include salads, fries, onion rings and housemade chili. Dessert options range from milkshakes and ice cream cones to banana splits, hot fudge sundaes and root beer floats.

799 Montecito Center, Santa Rosa, 707-538-0775. sites.google.com/bmaac.com/ozzies-grill

Superburger

Superburger traces its roots to the 1950s, when it opened in a small shack off Fourth Street in Santa Rosa. The longtime local institution still serves old-fashioned, char-grilled burgers from its original Fourth Street location, along with a second location in Cotati.

Over the years, Superburger expanded to locations in Cotati, Petaluma, Penngrove, Santa Rosa and Windsor. Most have since closed as the owner has returned the business to its roots.

The original Santa Rosa location has a 4.6-star DoorDash rating from more than 6,000 reviews. Its highest-rated items include beer-battered onion rings, the bacon-and-cheese Superburger and milkshakes.

The third-pound Black Angus burgers are char-grilled and served with a choice of cheese, lettuce, onion, tomato and pickles, plus Supersauce on soft potato buns. Superburger also serves third-pound, all-beef kosher hot dogs, including chili and Reuben dogs.

Beyond its burgers, the menu includes charbroiled chicken sandwiches, French dips and a sourdough patty melt. Sides include fries, tater tots, onion rings and pineapple coleslaw. There are also fresh-brewed iced teas and lemonades, along with more than 20 milkshake flavors.

1501 Fourth St., Santa Rosa, 707-546-4016; 8204 Old Redwood Highway, Cotati, 707-665-9790. originalsuperburger.com
